steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction to our paper on StyleTalker, a one-shot audio-driven talking head video generation model built on a style-based generator. Motivate the task, explain what previous one-shot methods get wrong, describe how our model works at a high level, and finish with a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: digital twins and audio-driven talking head generation
- Previous work and its limitations
- StyleTalker: style-based generator + GAN inversion, and the main challenge
- How we handle it: lip-sync discriminator, sequential VAE for motion, flow-augmented prior
- Inference modes and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - bridging real and virtual world with visual media increasingly important; coronavirus pandemic changed how we work, learn, play, socialize
  - digital twins: digital copies of real humans, realistic speech + facial expressions mimicking target; useful for virtual conferencing, VR/AR platforms
  - audio-driven talking head generation (synthesize video of talking person from input audio, multi-speaker) = crucial for digital twins
- Previous work
  - graphics works: realistic digital twins, but single-speaker, no control over multiple identities
  - one-shot audio-driven methods: single reference image + arbitrary audio; much attention, many applications
  - problems: only lip region, or no realistic motions (head pose, eye blinks) since modeling motion from audio is hard
  - Zhou et al.: pose-controllable, copies head poses from a given video independently of audio; but needs another video as pose source and misses eye blinks
- StyleTalker
  - novel audio-driven talking head generation model
  - style-based generator StyleGAN (rich distribution of faces) + GAN inversion to embed images in style latent space
  - style latent space: accurate facial attributes, disentangled; extensive image manipulation
  - generate video by sequentially estimating latent codes per frame
  - challenge: codes must reflect audio + motions and keep identity
- How we handle it
  - lip-sync discriminator pretrained with novel contrastive objective; fixed during training; improves lip sync
  - sequential VAE extracts motions from video; posterior of motion latent space conditioned on audio
  - auto-regressive prior + normalizing flow for complex audio-motion distributions
  - manipulate reference latent code: lip shapes, head poses, eye shapes per audio/motions; identity fixed
  - implicit representations; no geometry priors (landmarks, 3D pose parameters)
- Inference + contributions
  - sample from motion latent space (motion-controllable) or audio-to-motion latent space (audio-driven); Fig. 1
  - contributions: (a) novel one-shot framework controlling lips, head poses, eye blinks with pretrained image generator, unsupervised implicit representations; (b) motion-controllable or fully audio-driven generation; (c) state-of-art results, realistic videos, accurate lip sync, natural motions vs baselines, quantitative metrics + user studies

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recently it is becoming more and more important to bridge the gap between the real world and the virtual world with visual media, since the coronavirus pandemic has completely changed how we work, learn, play and socialize. This has led to digital twins, which are digital copies of real human beings that can generate realistic speech and facial expressions to mimic the target person. Digital twins are useful for real-world applications like virtual conferencing and VR/AR platforms. Audio-driven talking head generation, where the goal is to synthesize a video of a talking person from the input audio stream for multiple speakers, is a crucial technology to implement these digital twins.

Some previous works from graphics have had some success in generating realistic digital twins, but they target single-speaker generation, so they have no control over multiple identities. On the other hand, one-shot audio-driven talking head generation methods try to generate a talking head video from a single reference image of the target person and arbitrary audio. These methods have received a lot of attention recently because they can be applied in many applications. But the previous one-shot methods only synthesize the lip region, or they fail to predict realistic motions like head poses and eye blinks, because modeling motions from the audio is difficult. To overcome this, Zhou et al. recently proposed a pose-controllable method which copies the head poses of a given video independently from the given audio. But it is limited in its applicability because it needs another video as the pose source, and it also fails to capture facial attributes that are perceptually important, like eye blinks.

In this paper we propose StyleTalker, which is a new audio-driven talking head generation model. Our model uses a style-based generator, StyleGAN, which learns a rich distribution of human faces, and it uses GAN inversion techniques to embed images into the style latent space. It has been shown that the style latent space represents facial attributes accurately and with disentangled properties, which allows extensive image manipulations. We can generate a talking head video by estimating the latent codes of each frame in the video sequentially. But this is extremely challenging, because the estimated latent codes have to reflect the given audio and motions accurately while also keeping the identity, so that the talking head video is natural and realistic.

- handle challenge: lip-sync discriminator pretrained w/ novel contrastive objective, fixed during training -> better lip sync
- sequential VAE extracts motions from video; posterior of motion latent space conditioned on audio
- auto-regressive prior + normalizing flow for complicated audio/motion distributions
- manipulate reference latent code (lip shapes, head poses, eye shapes) per audio + motions, identity fixed; implicit representations, no landmarks / 3D pose parameters
- inference: sample from motion latent space (motion-controllable) or audio-to-motion latent space (audio-driven); Fig. 1
- contributions: one-shot framework controlling lips/head pose/eye blinks, unsupervised; motion-controllable or fully audio-driven; state-of-art, better lip sync + natural motions, metrics + user studies

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recently it is becoming more and more important to bridge the gap between the real world and the virtual world with visual media, since the coronavirus pandemic has completely changed how we work, learn, play and socialize. This has led to digital twins, which are digital copies of real human beings that can generate realistic speech and facial expressions to mimic the target person. Digital twins are useful for real-world applications like virtual conferencing and VR/AR platforms. Audio-driven talking head generation, where the goal is to synthesize a video of a talking person from the input audio stream for multiple speakers, is a crucial technology to implement these digital twins.

Some previous works from graphics have had some success in generating realistic digital twins, but they target single-speaker generation, so they have no control over multiple identities. On the other hand, one-shot audio-driven talking head generation methods try to generate a talking head video from a single reference image of the target person and arbitrary audio. These methods have received a lot of attention recently because they can be applied in many applications. But the previous one-shot methods only synthesize the lip region, or they fail to predict realistic motions like head poses and eye blinks, because modeling motions from the audio is difficult. To overcome this, Zhou et al. recently proposed a pose-controllable method which copies the head poses of a given video independently from the given audio. But it is limited in its applicability because it needs another video as the pose source, and it also fails to capture facial attributes that are perceptually important, like eye blinks.

In this paper we propose StyleTalker, which is a new audio-driven talking head generation model. Our model uses a style-based generator, StyleGAN, which learns a rich distribution of human faces, and it uses GAN inversion techniques to embed images into the style latent space. It has been shown that the style latent space represents facial attributes accurately and with disentangled properties, which allows extensive image manipulations. We can generate a talking head video by estimating the latent codes of each frame in the video sequentially. But this is extremely challenging, because the estimated latent codes have to reflect the given audio and motions accurately while also keeping the identity, so that the talking head video is natural and realistic.

To handle this challenge, first we pretrain our lip-sync discriminator with a new contrastive learning objective, and we use it as a fixed discriminator during training to improve lip synchronization with the input audio. We also extract motions from the video with a sequential variational autoencoder (VAE) to learn the posterior distribution of the motion latent space conditioned on the audio. On top of that, we design an auto-regressive prior augmented with normalizing flow, to capture more complicated probabilistic distributions between audio and possible motions. Then we manipulate the latent code of the reference image to change the lip shapes, head poses and eye shapes according to the given audio and motions, and reconstruct the video while the identity is kept fixed. This way our model learns implicit representations of them without any geometry priors like landmarks or 3D pose parameters.

So during inference, StyleTalker can generate realistic talking head videos by sampling the motions either from the motion latent space or from the audio-to-motion latent space. The first we call motion-controllable talking head video generation and the second audio-driven talking head video generation. Fig. 1 illustrates the overall concept of StyleTalker. Our contributions are summarized below.

- We propose StyleTalker, a new one-shot audio-driven talking head generation framework that controls lip movements, head poses and eye blinks with a pretrained image generator, by learning their implicit representations in an unsupervised way.

- StyleTalker can generate talking head videos in a motion-controllable way, with other videos as motion sources, or in a completely audio-driven way, where it predicts realistic motions from the audio.

- StyleTalker achieves state-of-art performance in talking head generation, and generates more realistic videos with accurate lip syncing and natural motions than baselines, both in quantitative metrics and in user studies.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Recently, bridging the gap between the real and the virtual world with visual media has become increasingly important, as the coronavirus pandemic has completely changed the way we work, learn, play, and socialize. This has led to the emergence of digital twins, digital copies of real human beings that can generate realistic speech and facial expressions to mimic the target person, which are useful for real-world applications such as virtual conferencing and VR/AR platforms. Audio-driven talking head generation, which aims to synthesize a video of a talking person from the input audio stream for multiple speakers, is a crucial technology for implementing such digital twins.

While some previous works from the graphics area [1,2,3] have achieved some success in generating realistic digital twins, they target single-speaker generation and thus have no control over multiple identities. One-shot audio-driven talking head generation methods [4,5,6,7], on the other hand, aim to generate a talking head video from a single reference image of the target person and arbitrary audio, and have recently received much attention due to their applicability. However, previous one-shot methods only synthesize the lip region [4] or fail to predict realistic motions (head poses and eye blinks) because of the difficulty of modeling motions from audio [5,6]. To overcome these issues, Zhou et al. [7] recently proposed a pose-controllable method that copies the head poses of a given video independently of the given audio, but its applicability is limited since it requires another video as the pose source, and it also fails to capture perceptually important facial attributes such as eye blinks.

In this paper, we propose StyleTalker, a novel audio-driven talking head generation model. Our model leverages a style-based generator, namely StyleGAN [8,9,10], which learns a rich distribution of human faces, and GAN inversion techniques [11,12] to embed images into the style latent space. The style latent space has been shown to represent facial attributes accurately with disentangled properties [11,12], allowing extensive image manipulations [13,14]. We can thus generate a talking head video by sequentially estimating the latent codes of each frame. However, this is extremely challenging, since the estimated latent codes should accurately reflect the given audio and motions while keeping the identity, in order to produce a natural and realistic talking head video.

To handle this challenge, we first pretrain our lip-sync discriminator with a novel contrastive learning objective and use it as a fixed discriminator during training to improve lip synchronization with the input audio. Furthermore, we extract motions from the video using a sequential variational autoencoder (VAE) [15] to learn the posterior distribution of the motion latent space conditioned on the audio. In addition, we design an auto-regressive prior augmented with normalizing flow to capture more complicated probabilistic distributions between audio and possible motions. We then manipulate the latent code of the reference image to change the lip shapes, head poses, and eye shapes according to the given audio and motions, reconstructing the video while keeping the identity fixed. In this way, our model learns their implicit representations without the help of geometry priors such as landmarks or 3D pose parameters.

As a result, during inference StyleTalker can generate realistic talking head videos by sampling the motions either from the motion latent space or from the audio-to-motion latent space. We refer to the former as motion-controllable and the latter as audio-driven talking head video generation. The overall concept of StyleTalker is illustrated in Fig. 1. Our contributions are summarized as follows.

- We propose StyleTalker, a novel one-shot audio-driven talking head generation framework that controls lip movements, head poses, and eye blinks using a pretrained image generator, by learning their implicit representations in an unsupervised manner.

- StyleTalker can generate talking head videos either in a motion-controllable manner, using other videos as motion sources, or in a completely audio-driven manner, predicting realistic motions from the audio.

- StyleTalker achieves state-of-art talking head generation performance, generating more realistic videos with accurate lip syncing and natural motions than the baselines, according to both quantitative metrics and user studies.
